When Trump's trade war with China was at its most intense, with tariffs escalating almost weekly, companies like Logitech promptly raised the prices of their products in the United States significantly.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the relevant tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. However, to date, no company has been seen passing on the refunds to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is currently underway to try to correct this situation...

The background to Trump's tariff saga

Last year, Trump seized on the U.S. trade deficit with China as a rallying point, clearly fantasising that imposing heavy taxes on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the United States.

Of course, this was never going to happen. The U.S. lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, specialised expertise, and cheap labour needed to make consumer electronics at the scale the major brands require.

Trump kept claiming that China paid the tariffs, but in reality the costs were borne by the American brands importing the finished goods, who then passed them on to consumers through price hikes. At the most chaotic point, tariffs had soared to 145%.

Take Logitech as an example — the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers should receive refunds

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to unilaterally impose tariffs, and stated that the amounts already paid by U.S. businesses must be refunded, with the relevant process currently underway.

The problem is that the costs were effectively borne by consumers through higher retail prices, yet so far no affected company has announced plans to refund customers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech on behalf of consumers who paid higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's take

In principle, this is completely uncontroversial. The companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra costs on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the companies. From a moral standpoint, the companies should return the corresponding proportion of funds to consumers who purchased the products during that period.

However, in practical terms, the process is likely to be extremely difficult. Logitech would need to identify every transaction across its vast network of third-party retailers, track how much each buyer paid, and calculate what portion of that constitutes the tariff cost.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it must be pointed out that in class-action lawsuits, the biggest beneficiaries are usually the lawyers, while the average compensation received by consumers is often very small.
